coming_in.species: Ducks, scaup, mergansers and geese, second segment
coming_in.method: Second segment of a three-way split
coming_in.dates: Oct. 3 to 11, Nov. 7 to 15, Dec. 21 to Jan. 31
coming_in.item: Two days out. The duck table's second segment opens Saturday, Nov. 7, and closes Sunday, Nov. 15, nine days of shooting, with the third segment Dec. 21 through Jan. 31; the first, Oct. 3 to 11, is closed, and both youth waterfowl days, Sept. 19 and Oct. 31, are past. The migratory summary's duck line reads daily bag six, possession 18, with the sub-limits in footnote (c): no more than four mallards, two of them hens, two black ducks, three pintails, three wood ducks, two redheads, two canvasbacks and four sea ducks, no more than three scoters and three long-tailed ducks among them; scaup, inside the duck bag, reads one per day Nov. 7 to 15 and Dec. 21 to Jan. 11 and two per day Jan. 12 to 31; coots run the same dates as ducks at 15 and 45, mergansers the same dates at five and 15 in aggregate, and gallinules' second segment opens Dec. 2. Canada and white-fronted geese and snow and blue geese share the Nov. 7 to 15 segment and a third Dec. 8 through Jan. 31, daily bag five and possession 15 in aggregate; brant open Jan. 2 at one and three. Shooting hours for waterfowl are one-half hour before sunrise to sunset, and HIP registration is required. The dates are not in the hunting and trapping pamphlet, which says so itself; they were re-read this morning from WVDNR's separate Migratory Bird Hunting Regulations Summary 2026-2027, which fetched through the proxy at 5:46 a.m. (HTTP 200, 1,940,942 bytes, md5 aad32d21343547146e3977a821a39355, identical to Wednesday's copy and the same size as every morning since Oct. 17, a 20th straight morning).

coming_in.species: Bobwhite quail, cottontail rabbit, snowshoe hare, ring-necked pheasant, red and gray fox, bobcat, and the furbearer trapping lines
coming_in.method: Hunting and trapping openers of Saturday, Nov. 7
coming_in.item: Two days out. Saturday, Nov. 7, is the pamphlet table's biggest opening day of the fall: bobwhite quail through Jan. 2, daily bag three, possession nine, closed on Tomblin WMA; cottontail rabbit through Feb. 28, daily bag five, possession 20; snowshoe hare through Feb. 28, daily bag two, possession eight; ring-necked pheasant, cock birds only, through Jan. 2, daily bag two, possession two, with the separate Hillcrest WMA line Nov. 14 to Dec. 5 at one, nine days out; raccoon trapping, and red and gray fox hunting and trapping, through Feb. 28; bobcat hunting and trapping through Feb. 28, season limit three, electronic registration required; and the trapping lines for mink and muskrat, skunk, opossum, coyote and weasel through Feb. 28, fisher and otter at a season limit of one each with registration, and beaver through March 31. The buck firearms season, Nov. 23 to Dec. 6, is 18 days out and stays outside the two-week window; the next antlerless deer and gun bear windows, both flagged selected counties with county lists not in the table, open the same day. The pamphlet is valid through June 30, 2027, checked against this morning's date.
coming_in.publication: West Virginia Hunting and Trapping Regulations Summary, July 2026 - June 2027

waters.reading: 54.9 cfs, 1.34 feet at 5:15 a.m., falling on discharge and steady on stage against 58.8 cfs and 1.37 feet in the fetcher's comparison.
waters.working: Down 1.3 cfs and 0.01 feet on the day against the USGS trace's 56.2 cfs and 1.35 feet at 5:15 a.m. Wednesday, Wednesday's edition reading, a 19th straight falling morning and the smallest drop of the recession: 103 Tuesday of last week, 94 Wednesday, 85 Thursday, 79 Friday, 73 Saturday, 66 Sunday, 62 Monday, 59 Tuesday, 56 Wednesday, 55 today, drops of 9, 8, 6, 6, 7, 4, 3, 3 and 1. The rain that fell on the Ohio valley Wednesday has not reached this gauge: the trace is the same stair-step, 56.2 through Wednesday morning, flickering 56.2 and 54.9 between 10:15 and 11:30 a.m., 54.9 through the afternoon and evening with one 53.7 reading at 7:45 p.m., a 56.2 blip at 4 a.m. and 54.9 since 4:30 a.m., the stage sliding 1.35 to 1.34 at the same breaks and touching 1.33 once at 7:45 p.m., no bump anywhere in it. The read string is the fetcher's own verdict, printed as it stands, "55 cfs - prime wading water.", and its 58.8 cfs and 1.37 feet comparison points are Tuesday morning's values on the trace, not Wednesday's, about 48 hours old for the fourth straight day, so the 3.9-cfs drop they imply is two days' worth; the falling flag on discharge is right in direction and the steady flag on stage is the fetcher's band verdict on a 0.03-foot change. The Ohio gauges' rain buckets show what Wednesday delivered downstream, hundredths of an inch at a time from late morning through the evening at Point Pleasant, 0.11 inch in the quarter hour to 10 p.m. the largest, and 0.07 to 0.09 inch a quarter hour at Huntington between 6 and 6:30 p.m., nothing at either since 11 p.m.; the Huntington airport's observations through 5:10 a.m. read cloudy, 63 to 64F, no precipitation in the past hour. Whether any of it fell on the Williams headwaters, and when the gauge shows it, is Friday's trace to read; this morning the river is at the lowest point of its 19-day recession. Stocking: WVDNR's fall program, announced Oct. 19, was the weeks of Oct. 19 and 26, one stocking per water each week, and the agency's fish-stocking page, which fetched through the proxy this morning, carries an empty list under "The following waters were stocked:"; the river's most recent stocking this paper has reported is still Thursday, Oct. 29, from WVNS's Oct. 29 list, and WVNS's Oct. 30 list, published Friday at 5:12 p.m. and still the newest on its fishing-and-hunting feed at 5:48 a.m., does not name the Williams, the Cranberry or the Summersville tailwater, with no list dated Oct. 31 or any day of November on that feed, so Thursday's fish have had a week to spread out of the first pools below the truck stops. At 55 cfs and clear the pocket water, plunge pools and undercut banks the file records as its structure hold less water than on any morning of the recession, the wading is easy everywhere, and the fish are pinned to what current is left, the heads and tongues of the plunge pools, the single deep slot in each run of pocket water and the shade under the cut banks, where they see a wader from a long way off. This is a long-leader, small-fly problem, more so than Wednesday, and the overcast is the one thing in the river's favor: a 12-foot leader to 6X or 7X, a size 20 to 22 blue-winged olive or a small parachute Adams on top through the middle of the day, cloud being the light the olives come off in, a size 18 or 20 pheasant tail or zebra midge dropped 18 inches under it through the morning for the caddis and small stonefly nymphs the file records as forage, and a size 10 olive sculpin pattern or a small black woolly bugger swung slow and deep through the plunge pools toward dusk, the one heavier fly the low water allows and one the stocked fish take too; an egg pattern or a bright San Juan worm under a small indicator covers the holdover stocked pools without changing the rig. If the river comes up stained on Wednesday's rain, that rig gives way to a heavier nymph on the seams, and the gauge will say so before anyone on the bank does.

waters.near: 14 miles above R.C. Byrd Locks and Dam
waters.reading: 24.44 feet at 5 a.m., falling against 24.95 in the fetcher's comparison.
waters.read: 24.4 ft and falling — normal pool. Ordinary bank access.
waters.working: The fetcher reads the pool falling, 0.51 under its 24.95 comparison point, and this morning the direction is right for the day as well: against Wednesday's 5 a.m. reading of 25.03, Wednesday's edition reading, the gauge is down 0.59, the biggest one-day move at this gauge in a week. The trace held between 25.0 and 25.2 all Wednesday, 25.20 at 1 p.m. and again at 3:15 p.m., 25.09 at 7 p.m., 25.04 at 9 p.m., then drained through the night, 24.92 at 11 p.m., 24.85 at midnight, 24.73 at 1 a.m., 24.58 at 3 a.m., 24.44 at 4:15 a.m. and 24.44 at 5 a.m., 0.6 feet in eight hours with no rain in the bucket since 11 p.m. and the Williams still falling, so the drop is the pool being drawn down through the dam, not the river running off; the gauge below says where it went. The rain itself was real but small: the Point Pleasant gauge's own bucket ticked hundredths from 10:15 a.m. through the evening, 0.11 inch in the quarter hour to 10 p.m. the largest. The read string is the fetcher's band verdict, normal pool, ordinary bank access, and at 24.4 the gauge is 2.6 feet under the up-and-pushing line at 27 feet. A pool drawn down half a foot overnight and still clear fishes the structure, with a little more of it showing than Wednesday: shad are the forage and the skipjack are with them, so a white or pearl swimbait on a half-ounce head or a three-quarter-ounce spoon worked down the current face of each wing dam and along the riprap at first light for the hybrids and white bass pushing bait against the rock, a crawfish-colored jig or a three-inch tube dragged slow on the riprap for smallmouth and drum once the day's light is on the water, and, with the river cooling into November and the drawdown adding a little pull through the pool, a half-ounce blade bait or a jig and minnow worked vertical along the lock wall's seam and the edges of the barge cuts, where the sauger stack as the water cools; cut skipjack on the bottom in the barge cuts after dark for blue catfish. The slack behind the dams is for when the river colours, and the trace shows no colour this morning.

waters.near: below R.C. Byrd Locks and Dam
waters.reading: 26.29 feet at 5 a.m., steady against 26.42 in the fetcher's comparison.
waters.read: 26.3 ft — normal pool. Ordinary bank access.
waters.working: The fetcher reads the gauge steady, 0.13 under its 26.42 comparison point, but that point is a Tuesday-morning value on the trace, about 48 hours old for the fourth straight day, not Wednesday's 5 a.m. reading of 26.02, Wednesday's edition reading; against that the gauge is up 0.27 on the day, and the steady flag is wrong in direction for the day. The overnight pool transfer that did not come Tuesday night came Wednesday night: the trace sat between 25.96 and 26.16 through Wednesday, started up at about 9:45 p.m. at 26.20, 26.26 at 11:30 p.m., 26.29 at 1:15 a.m., 26.31 at 2:45 a.m., 26.35 at 4 a.m. and 26.29 at 5 a.m., 0.71 under the 27-foot line between normal pool and up and pushing, while the pool above it at Point Pleasant fell 0.6 over the same hours. The dam below tells the same story: the USGS gauge on the Ohio at Ironton, Ohio, below Greenup Dam, the next dam down, recorded Greenup's discharge at 21,100 cfs at 6 a.m. Wednesday, building through the day to 30,000 to 31,600 by 4 p.m., a 35,700 peak at 6:30 p.m., 28,000 to 33,000 through the night and 27,900 at 5 a.m. today, a third more than Wednesday morning, with the Ironton stage up from 34.29 to 34.51 over the same 24 hours. So the pattern this paper has watched since Sunday is three nights out of four: the Byrd pool drawn down overnight, Huntington's pool up a few tenths, Greenup passing more by morning; whether it is scheduled or a lockage pattern the traces still do not say, and this paper will not guess. Wednesday's rain was small here too, the Huntington gauge's bucket catching 0.07 to 0.09 inch a quarter hour between 6 and 6:30 p.m. and nothing since 10 p.m. The read string is the fetcher's band verdict, normal pool, ordinary bank access. Water below the dam up 0.3 and with Greenup passing a third more than Wednesday has a little more current on the seams, and the fishing goes to them: the forage is shad and skipjack with crawfish in the riprap, so a white swimbait or a three-quarter-ounce spoon down the current face of each wing dam at first light, a half-ounce blade bait or a chartreuse-and-white paddletail on a half-ounce head worked slow along the lock wall's seam for the sauger, which hold on the wall's downstream edge whatever the dam is passing and feed better with the push on, a crawfish jig dragged on the riprap through the cloudy middle of the day, and cut skipjack on the bottom in the slack beside the dam's discharge for blue and flathead catfish after dark, with the current moving the bait to them tonight.

waters.reading: Sound at Hampstead: high 4:38 AM at 3.9 ft, low 11:09 AM at 0.5 ft, high 5:00 PM at 3.8 ft, low 11:30 PM at 0.3 ft. Surf at Ocean City Beach pier: high 4:06 AM at 4.9 ft, low 10:17 AM at 0.5 ft, high 4:24 PM at 4.5 ft, low 10:27 PM at 0.3 ft. Water 66.6F at Beaufort, 60 miles up the coast, observed 5:30 a.m. Moon waning crescent, 21% lit, 25.1 days old.
waters.read: Fish the moving water either side of high at 4:38 AM and 5:00 PM in the sound.
waters.working: The sound topped out at 4:38 a.m. and is just starting to drain at press time, an hour into the ebb toward the 11:09 a.m. low, so the whole morning is falling water, and the first of it is the fetcher's own window, the moving water either side of the high. Waning crescent: the fetcher's file carries the moon at 21 percent lit and 25.1 days old, four or five days short of new, so the swings are building toward the spring tides around the new moon; the file's ranges show it, the surf's morning high at 4.9 feet against Wednesday's 4.5, the sound's morning high 3.9 against 3.8 and its late low 0.3 against 0.4, a 3.4-foot drain this morning and a 3.5-foot drain tonight. All four of the sound's events at Hampstead land inside today, and all four of the surf's do too: a 3.9-foot high at 4:38 a.m., a drain to a 0.5-foot low at 11:09 a.m., a fill of 3.3 feet to the 3.8-foot high at 5 p.m., and a drain to a 0.3-foot low at 11:30 p.m. The surf at Ocean City Beach pier runs ahead and is the bigger water: high 4:06 a.m. at 4.9, low 10:17 a.m. at 0.5, high 4:24 p.m. at 4.5, low 10:27 p.m. at 0.3, so the sound lags the surf by 32 and 36 minutes on the highs and 52 and 63 minutes on the lows, the long-lag-on-the-ebb pattern the reference describes. Beaufort's thermometer, 60 miles up the coast, read 66.6F at 5:30 a.m., up 0.9 on the day and the second straight morning of warming after four days of cooling. What's running comes from a live report: the Fisherman's Post Topsail/Sneads Ferry November report, published Sunday, Nov. 1, at 8 a.m. Eastern, four days old this morning, inside the 21-day gate; it is a monthly report and describes the fishing of the past week or two, not today's water. The Jolly Roger Pier reports scattered speckled trout starting to show at the pier, that "Bottom fishing action has been better at night," with good-sized Virginia mullet and spot, and that "Bluefish have been pretty thick, especially in the early mornings"; the Surf City Pier reports pompano, black drum and croakers on the bottom, casting shots at Spanish mackerel and bluefish, and that "King mackerel fishing was really good before this last blow." East Coast Sports has the piers catching a few big red drum over 32 inches, mostly on the island's north end, kings in double digits a day off the piers before the wind, Spanish and bluefish slowed by the rough water, and the sound giving smaller reds and the occasional trout with the focus shifting almost entirely to trout as it cools; Native Son says the wind has pushed the bait around, wants cut bait over artificials for the inside reds, and for trout says to "focus on the deeper seams (5-8')" in the main creeks; Speckled Specialist is on numbers of smaller trout with fish to 28 inches mixed in, black drum to 18 inches over structure and smaller reds, most in 4 to 8 feet of water, on live shrimp under a cork and 3/16-ounce jigheads with soft plastics; Carolina Flats is scouting trout schools early on topwater, dropping to the deeper holes later in the day, and expects a last blitz of reds on the oyster and grass banks on soft plastics before the bait thins inshore. That squares with the reference calendar's November pattern, speckled trout prime with red drum, bluefish, spot and sea mullet. Tide is the whole game here, and the report's trout are the fish on the structure the file records: a topwater plug over the grass edges at first light with the ebb just starting, the window the report's guides use to find the schools, then a 3/16- or quarter-ounce jighead with a paddletail or a soft jerkbait worked slow along the grass edges and down the 5- to 8-foot drop into the ICWW channel as the drain finishes toward 11:09 a.m., a popping cork with live shrimp over the oyster bars on the first of the flood behind the low and again on either side of the 5 p.m. high, and the same plastics or a suspending twitchbait under the dock lights after dark on the evening ebb, where the finger mullet, shrimp and mud minnows stack up. Red drum want the last of the fall, and today that comes twice, both windows later than Wednesday's: in daylight from about 9 a.m. to the 11:09 a.m. low, and after dark from about 9:30 p.m. to the 11:30 p.m. low, cut menhaden or a finger mullet on a quarter-ounce jighead fan-cast a couple of feet off the creek-channel edges as the grass drains, with the top of the flood around 5 p.m., right at dusk, the look at drum on the flooded grass and oyster banks, a weedless gold spoon or a soft plastic worked over the edges. Spot and sea mullet on bloodworm or shrimp on a two-hook bottom rig in the ICWW channel an hour either side of the 5 p.m. high, and the piers' night bottom bite says the same rig works after dark on the ebb. Bluefish are a metal jig or a topwater plug behind the bait pods on the beach in the early morning, the piers' and the report's best window for them. NWS Wilmington, read at 5:46 a.m.: a Special Weather Statement issued at 4:58 a.m. EST covers Coastal Pender among a list of Carolina zones, for patchy fog that may become locally dense and cut visibility under a quarter mile on area roadways, expiring at 8 a.m.; the same statement, a second morning running, and the only product on the zone.
